content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper presents a new method SARNet for multiagent communication which uses ideas from transformers as well as MAC to perform better than baselines. The model first extracts out important stuff from current information (broadcasted communication from other agents as well own private observation) and then extract important information from previous memories it has relevant to current step. The model is trained using centralized learning and decentralized execution approach. Then, paper empirically shows better results than baselines on OpenAI’s multi-agent particle environment.

The paper is well written and the flow is easy to read. The SARNet is usually better in larger scale experiments but it is hard to say if it will generalize to other environments as all experiments are on multi-agent particle environment. Therefore, due to lack of clear positive signal from few experiments and issues mentioned below, I provide an initial rating of weak reject which I would be happy to increase once following concerns are resolved. 

For a proper comparison, it would be good to compare the number of parameters as well as plots for rewards and convergence with respect to baselines. Are the parameters among the agents shared in any way? 

How many runs were used for the final runs? From the paper, it seems like it is only one run which won’t capture variance. [1] which came between CommNet and TarMAC is missing from baselines. Using [1] will allow SARNet to be extended to non-cooperative settings. Also, the setup optimizes global rewards, but [1] shows that individualizing the rewards helps in overall performance. It would be great to know if individualized rewards can help SARNet further.

An ablation that is missing from the paper is one where you only use memory unit and disable the attention mechanism. It would give a signal on how much memory helps. The paper is missing proper qualitative analysis on what agents communicate and if there are some sort of common signals there. Analysis like the ones in CommNet [2] paper would be helpful to understand what is being communicated. Surprisingly, in 4.4, MC-SARNet is performing better on #Captures ‘N’, any explanations on that. Do the titles of table in Table 3 need to be exchanged? 

Also, how is the mean reward getting calculated in partially observable physical deception task? I didn’t understand that which confused me about Table 2(b) and results for section 4.3. The gap between Average distance for CommNet and SARNet is huge for N=3, but SARNet performs better for N=6. It is hard to derive a conclusion based on just these two. What happens when N=9 is tested, does SARNet again beat the baselines. If it does, we can make a more solid claim about performance. Same goes for the rest of the tasks.Section 4.3 is only evaluated on one setting and Section 4.2 is only evaluated on N=3 and N=6.

I find the metrics for the particles environment a little coarse which might be adding noise to the overall signal. Something like Traffic Junction provides clear signal on the improvements.

Typos/Clarification:

3.1 Through a structured reasoning
3.1 the model interacts with memories -> Are memories shared in communication directly?
Page 4: The key and value are broadcasted
I might be missing something but are the dimensions of a_i^t and similar variables correct, it seems like they should R^{NxQ}
Table 3(a) - Memory in predator-prey

[1] Singh, Amanpreet, Tushar Jain, and Sainbayar Sukhbaatar. "Learning when to communicate at scale in multiagent cooperative and competitive tasks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.09755 (2018).
[2] Sukhbaatar, Sainbayar, and Rob Fergus. "Learning multiagent communication with backpropagation." In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, pp. 2244-2252. 2016.

content.title: Response to Review #3
content.comment:
Thank you so much for your constructive comments on our work. Our response is noted below - 

> ”1. For a proper comparison, it would be good to compare the number of parameters as well as plots for rewards and convergence with respect to baselines. Are the parameters among the agents shared in any way? “

All the parameters are shared across the agents in the communication architecture. Moreover, we also use comparable parameter settings for all baselines. For example, the action units, and communication vectors in SARNet and TarMAC both 128 units and 16/32 units respectively. This has been described in the Appendix under the Experiments/Baseline section.

> “2. How many runs were used for the final runs? From the paper, it seems like it is only one run which won’t capture variance. [1] which came between CommNet and TarMAC is missing from baselines. Using [1] will allow SARNet to be extended to non-cooperative settings. Also, the setup optimizes global rewards, but [1] shows that individualizing the rewards helps in overall performance. It would be great to know if individualized rewards can help SARNet further.”

We tested the architecture over 3 separate runs with distinct random seeds. Additionally, the trained policies were benchmarked over 100,000 steps. The training graph is setup in such a way that individual critics train each agents policy individually. Each agent’s policy maintains a copy of the other agent’s communication framework that is necessary to receive the key and value vectors. This setup allows our architecture to be trained in non-cooperative settings, and also with individual rewards that are not shared, without the use of [1]. However, [1] would allow SARNet to potentially scale to large number of agents, or in cases where the communication bandwidth is limited.

> “3. An ablation that is missing from the paper is one where you only use memory unit and disable the attention mechanism. It would give a signal on how much memory helps. The paper is missing proper qualitative analysis on what agents communicate and if there are some sort of common signals there. Analysis like the ones in CommNet [2] paper would be helpful to understand what is being communicated. Surprisingly, in 4.4, MC-SARNet is performing better on #Captures ‘N’, any explanations on that. Do the titles of table in Table 3 need to be exchanged? “

The error is noted. The table should be for cooperative navigation, wherein the Column 1 would read # of collisions (lower the better), and Average Distance (lower the better), for cooperative navigation with 6 agents. This has been corrected in the revision.

> “4. Also, how is the mean reward getting calculated in partially observable physical deception task? I didn’t understand that which confused me about Table 2(b) and results for section 4.3. The gap between Average distance for CommNet and SARNet is huge for N=3, but SARNet performs better for N=6. It is hard to derive a conclusion based on just these two. What happens when N=9 is tested, does SARNet again beat the baselines. If it does, we can make a more solid claim about performance. Same goes for the rest of the tasks.Section 4.3 is only evaluated on one setting and Section 4.2 is only evaluated on N=3 and N=6.”

Due to the physical deception being an inherently harder task, upon introducing an additional “good agent”, we face convergence issues for the DDPG agents. This is mainly due to the environment being unbounded and the DDPG agents tend to drift away from the environment screen. The issue with convergence has also been noted in the original MADDPG paper, where the environment has been introduced. We will consider including larger number of agents in our evaluation for future work.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
Summary:
The paper deals with the problem of training cooperative agents in a multi-agent reinforcement learning setting. The agents are given the ability to communicate with each other and are trained using the centralized training, decentralized execution paradigm. 

Architecture has been proposed that: (i) attends to relevant communication messages received by an agent using an attention mechanism similar to the one proposed in [1]; and (ii) endows each agent with a memory. The authors argue that memory assists the agents in performing explicit reasoning.

The proposed architecture consists of four units:
1. Thought unit for processing local observation to obtain query, key and value vectors along with an observation encoding.
2. Question unit for obtaining an attention distribution over all agents (using one's own query vector and the [key, vector] pairs received from all agents) via a modified version of attention mechanism proposed in [1].
3. Memory unit for using the attention weights obtained in step 2 to update agents memory
4. Action unit for picking action based on agent's memory and local observation.

Experiments done with cooperative agents on three different tasks from multi-agent particle environments show that in some cases the proposed architecture outperforms other approaches. Two experiments that aim to understand the role of attention and memory have also been performed.


Comments:
1. The Introduction section lacks motivation. An example to explain terms like structured reasoning would help a lot.

2. At least to me, it is not apparent how the memory or attention leads to an "explicit" reasoning process.

3. In section 2.1 A_i and O_i are sets and not actions or observations respectively.

4. On p5, in the paragraph before Section 3.3, it is written that "... it learns to assign importance to each element in the information vector.". Further clarification is needed here. As the weights act on the entire vector in the memory unit, the statement appears to be a bit misleading.

5. The current setup requires the key-value pairs to be broadcasted to all agents. This would be inefficient when a large number of agents are present - which is essentially the case where one would want to filter out information using such an approach.

The paper is overloaded with terminology that can be avoided and the presentation can be simplified. There is redundancy in writing and many statements are vague, e.g., the one that talks about performing explicit structured reasoning. The description can be condensed and space can be used for more informative ablation studies.


Questions to the Authors:
See the comments above.


References:
[1] Vaswani et al., 2017, Attention is all you need.

display_title: Response to Review #1 for Comments (1, 2, 4) and 5.

content.title: Response to Review #1 for Comments (1, 2, 4) and 5.
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback on our work. Our responses are noted below - 

> “1. The Introduction section lacks motivation. An example to explain terms like structured reasoning would help a lot.”
&
> “2. At least to me, it is not apparent how the memory or attention leads to an "explicit" reasoning process.”
&
> “4. On p5, in the paragraph before Section 3.3, it is written that "... it learns to assign importance to each element in the information vector.". Further clarification is needed here. As the weights act on the entire vector in the memory unit, the statement appears to be a bit misleading.”

- To briefly describe the reasoning process, we take a look at the communication architecture. Each agent receives a set of vectors from the other communicating agents, a Key and a Value. The agent then computes a weighted interaction between the keys and the query that it generates. This allows the agent to learn the importance of the information from each agent that is being received. Furthermore, the interaction of the value vectors and the current memory of the agent is computed to reason how correlated the information received is. For example, if  a particular element in the value vector of agent ‘j’ is of a high value, and respective element in the receiving agent ‘i’’s memory is higher, a higher importance will be placed on that. This is governed by the interaction through the Hadamard Product. Moreover, a linear projection, over the previous result, regulates the weighting of each element in the final vector with respect to each other. This relational computation between the information from other agents, and it's own memories, governs the reasoning process behind every action.

 > “5. The current setup requires the key-value pairs to be broadcasted to all agents. This would be inefficient when a large number of agents are present - which is essentially the case where one would want to filter out information using such an approach. The paper is overloaded with terminology that can be avoided and the presentation can be simplified. There is redundancy in writing and many statements are vague, e.g., the one that talks about performing explicit structured reasoning. The description can be condensed and space can be used for more informative ablation studies.”

For future work we plan to explore a scalable approach to this system, similar to how IC3Net is developed.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The authors propose a multi-agent communication framework(SARNet) using memory-based attention network. The main framework is to facilitate inter-agent communication and prior
information to help decision.

Main issues:
1. In the Introduction part, the author claim the TarMAC does not use memory in the communication step, however TarMAC uses GRU policy to generate action and message, it does use the memory to generate message. So maybe you should look up it again.
2. The main framework is so similar to TarMAC, I can hardly to conclude the novelty in this paper. Can you make a more detailed comparisons with TarMAC? Can the Questiion Unit be considered as the Targeted Communication part in TarMAC? If so, the main difference between SARNet and TarMAC is they use different ways to aggregate information in Memory Unit?
3. For the experiment part, there need more figures and analysis. I think there may be need some learning curve figure or the final reward to prove the SARNet outperformed baselines. For example, in POCN, the agents are guided by dense reward, the the reward do measure the performance. The paper just provided the collisions and average dist in the environment, which is a good way to analysis emergent behavior but not enough to evaluate the algorithm. The attention visualization in Figure3 should place the correspond scene to demonstrator the learnt attention is meaningful. The main contribution from my perspective is the Memory Unit, however the paper just do the ablation study with noise in memory unit, this is not enough. The noise in memory part can be reasoned to the robustness problem in neural network also. You can test whether agents choose different strategies for same situation when their experience is different.

display_title: Response to Review #2 about comparisons to TarMAC

content.title: Response to Review #2 about comparisons to TarMAC
content.comment:
Thank you for the insightful feedback on our work. Our responses are noted below - 

> “1. In the Introduction part, the author claim the TarMAC does not use memory in the communication step, however TarMAC uses GRU policy to generate action and message, it does use the memory to generate message. So maybe you should look up it again.”

We agree that we should have been more clear in our comparison of the communication architecture in TarMAC. Our understanding of TarMAC is that, the communication is essentially utilizes dot-product attention. The memory from the GRU, implicitly is used to aggregate information specific to each agent. However, TarMAC does not use any explicit memory in their communication architecture. It is only the choice of their policy network (GRU), which allows them to aggregate information. For example, if the policy network is replaced with an MLP (depending on the task), there would be not memory in the communication. 

> “2. The main framework is so similar to TarMAC, I can hardly to conclude the novelty in this paper. Can you make a more detailed comparisons with TarMAC? Can the Questiion Unit be considered as the Targeted Communication part in TarMAC? If so, the main difference between SARNet and TarMAC is they use different ways to aggregate information in Memory Unit? “

The targeted communication part mainly consists of three components, the Query, Keys and Values. This is an adaptation of the widely popular dot-product attention from the Transformer network used in NLP/QVA. TarMAC uses the stock dot-product attention mechanism for the communication method, wherein, the Queries, Keys and Values from timestep ‘t’ compute the message for the next timestep ‘t+1’.

In SARNet, the first underlying difference, is that communication message generated in timestep ‘t’, is used to influence the ‘action’ in the same timestep. Each agent generates a Query, Key and Value, akin to how TarMAC does. The way the computation for the new message is done is entirely different - 

For the Question Unit, TarMAC does a dot-product over the Query and Keys. However, in our architecture we perform a weighted dot-product, that is we calculate the question, through a linear projection of the Hadamard Product. This allows the agent to learn the importance of each element in the Question, with respect to the other information present in the question vector, similar to a reasoning process.

For the Memory Unit, TarMAC again uses a dot-product over its value generated in the Question Unit, and that with the Keys. Note here, there is no memory generated nor used for this operation in the communication. In SARNet, however, the agent maintains a copy of the communication memory, and the Values received from each agent are first compared to the memory of the agent. This allows the agent to reason with the new information received, and generate a new set of Values, that is then used to compute the final message. Again, we use a weighted dot-product (i.e. a linear projection, to regulate importance).

> “3. For the experiment part, there need more figures and analysis. I think there may be need some learning curve figure or the final reward to prove the SARNet outperformed baselines. For example, in POCN, the agents are guided by dense reward, the the reward do measure the performance. The paper just provided the collisions and average dist in the environment, which is a good way to analysis emergent behavior but not enough to evaluate the algorithm. The attention visualization in Figure3 should place the correspond scene to demonstrator the learnt attention is meaningful. The main contribution from my perspective is the Memory Unit, however the paper just do the ablation study with noise in memory unit, this is not enough. The noise in memory part can be reasoned to the robustness problem in neural network also. You can test whether agents choose different strategies for same situation when their experience is different.”

We describe how the rewards are calculated based on the number of collisions and average distance for each specific environment. We also agree with your assessment on the study on the memory unit, and attention values over the complete episodic step.
